Per-link audit log · 5005 changes on 457 links

Every change to every link.

Each row below is one field of one link that changed in one release, with its old value, its new value and the reason where one is recorded. Releases are listed newest first.

Framework (methods)Download the log as CSVReferences

How the checks were run. The author ran the checks with AI-assisted verification. AI models compared each filed estimate with the paper it cites, and the author reviewed the results and applied the corrections. The method and its limits are in the framework.

How this log is made. A script reads the published page of every release and compares it with the release before. It writes one row for each field that changed on each link, and one row for each link added or removed. The reason comes from the reviewer’s note on the link, the correction record in the dataset repository, and (from version 2.0) the grade basis. Where none is recorded, the row shows the release message. Rule ids such as T3 or C1 refer to the decision table in the framework.

Reading the grades. Before version 2.0 the grades were called Convincing, Probable, Suggestive, Limited and Contested. They are now Strong, Moderate, Suggestive, Weak and Conflicting. The log lists a grade change only when the level moved. Translated texts are left out. Each link has an anchor: changelog.html#risk|disease.

Version 2.023 Oct 2026

release b1a4cda · 431 links · 431 changed

Chronic Disease Evidence Explorer v2.0: grading reform

Grade names changed on 255 links (Convincing to Strong, Probable to Moderate, Limited to Weak, Contested to Conflicting). The rows below list only changes of level.

Disease renamed: Major depression to Depression.

Disease renamed: Osteoporotic fracture to Fracture in adults.

Disease renamed: Chronic low back pain to Back pain.

Grade moves: 54 Probable to Suggestive; 16 Suggestive to Weak; 10 Convincing to Moderate; 2 Limited to Suggestive; 1 Probable to Weak; 1 Suggestive to Moderate.

Rows by field: Measure 431, Estimate source 431, Estimate design 431, Outcome match 431, Outcome measured 431, Trial and genetic evidence 431, Score (ESS) 289, Effective reviews (N_eff) 202, Reviews counted 184, Grade basis 173, Sources 121, Grade 84, Related outcome 75, Adjudicating bodies 64, External grades 50, Grade override 40, Conflict 24, Rests on primary studies 21, Studies 21, I-squared 6, Caveat 6, Estimate 4, Interval, lower 4, Interval, upper 4, Comparison 4, Comparison type 4, Quoted sentence 4, ci_low_exact 3, Mediation note 1.

Standard reasons in this release. The fields below carry the same reason on every link. The CSV repeats it on each row.

Measure. Added in version 2.0: the measure behind the estimate (RR, HR, OR, SMR or rate ratio) is stored and shown beside it. Framework section 3.3.

Estimate source. Added in version 2.0: the source that carries the displayed estimate is recorded. Rules T4 and T5 and the counting rule read it. Framework section 7.

Estimate design. Added in version 2.0: the design behind the displayed estimate is recorded. Rules T4, T5a to T5d and the Mendelian randomisation position read it. Framework section 7.

Score (ESS). The score is recomputed from the estimate, the effective review number (N_eff) and the grade weight: 100 x M x R x C. Framework section 3.4.

Trial and genetic evidence. Version 2.0 stores trial and genetic evidence as records with their sources and the checks "same exposure" and "same outcome". Rules T2, T3, C1 and C3 read them. The status of each is unchanged. Framework section 9.

Adjudicating bodies. Added in version 2.0: the bodies that rated this pair are recorded, with whether each rating matches this pair. Rules T3, T4 and T9 read them. Framework section 10.2.

External grades. Added in version 2.0: ratings of this pair by outside systems are recorded. Rule T11 reads them. Framework section 3.2.3.

Conflict. Added in version 2.0: the two sides of the disagreement and their sources are recorded for a Conflicting link. Rule C2 reads them. Framework section 3.2.3.

Score (ESS). A link in the related-outcome layer carries no score. Framework section 6.4.

Conflict
Side A: A genetic analysis supports a causal role: variants that raise triglycerides raise coronary artery disease after…
Side A: A genetic analysis supports a causal role: variants that raise triglycerides raise coronary artery disease after accounting for LDL and HDL cholesterol (Do 2013). Side B: A pooled analysis of 302,430 people found no independent association once HDL and non-HDL cholesterol were accounted for (hazard ratio 0.99, 0.94 to 1.05). Comparison, Comparison type, Caveat, Quoted sentence: INTERSTROKE reports regular physical activity at 0.60 (99% CI 0.52-0.70) for all stroke, whose reciprocal is 1.67 (1.43-1.92) for inactivity - considerably larger than the 1.26 on file. This is a case-control odds ratio with 99% intervals and is vulnerable to reverse causation and recall bias, so the true cohort value probably lies between the two; the dose-response cohort literature finds most of the benefit accrues by 8.75 mMET-hours/week, equivalent to the recommended 150 minutes. Pooled from 11 prospective studies; heavy drinking raised intracerebral haemorrhage more than ischaemic stroke in the sa…
Pooled from 11 prospective studies; heavy drinking raised intracerebral haemorrhage more than ischaemic stroke in the same analysis. A second synthesis (Zhang 2014, 27 prospective studies) found no significant effect of heavy drinking on haemorrhagic stroke. Mendelian randomisation in East Asian populations shows a clear, monotonic increase in stroke with alcohol, with no protective threshold.
Quoted sentence
For stroke, genotype-predicted mean alcohol intake had a continuously positive log-linear association with risk, which w…
For stroke, genotype-predicted mean alcohol intake had a continuously positive log-linear association with risk, which was stronger for intracerebral haemorrhage (relative risk [RR] per 280 g per week 1.58, 95% CI 1.36-1.84, p<0.0001) than for ischaemic stroke (1.27, 1.13-1.43, p=0.0001).
High alcohol consumption (>2-4 drinks/day) was associated with a non-significant increased risk of both hemorrhagic stro…
High alcohol consumption (>2-4 drinks/day) was associated with a non-significant increased risk of both hemorrhagic stroke subtypes, and the relative risk for heavy drinking (>4 drinks/day) were 1.67 (95 % CI, 1.25-2.23) for intracerebral hemorrhage and 1.82 (95 % CI, 1.18-2.82) for subarachnoid hemorrhage.

Grade basis
Conflicting (rule C2): observational studies and two genetic analyses point to protection, while the Danish ease-of-quit…
Conflicting (rule C2): observational studies and two genetic analyses point to protection, while the Danish ease-of-quitting study supports reverse causation in the years before diagnosis. The genetic studies were designed to test reverse causation and still found protection, so the owner should decide whether Conflicting still fits. Without the conflict record the table finds no ceiling for this link.
Conflict
Side A: Cohort and case-control studies over several decades find fewer cases of Parkinson's disease in current smokers…
Side A: Cohort and case-control studies over several decades find fewer cases of Parkinson's disease in current smokers (0.39, 0.32 to 0.47), and two Mendelian randomisation studies support a protective effect of smoking (0.74 per standard deviation of smoking initiation; 0.64 for continued smoking against quitting). Side B: A Danish case-control study found that people who later developed Parkinson's disease had quit smoking more easily than controls, which suggests that the earliest changes of the disease weaken the urge to smoke and that part of the association runs the other way (Ritz 2014). Sources: hernan_smoking_coffee_pd_2002 domenighetti2022_pd_mr dominguez2021_pd_mr ritz2014_pd_quitting

Moderate: the displayed estimate is one Mendelian randomisation analysis of BMI on sleep apnoea, and the genetic evidenc…
Moderate: the displayed estimate is one Mendelian randomisation analysis of BMI on sleep apnoea, and the genetic evidence meets rule T3. The other synthesis cited (Esmaeili 2025) pools the prevalence of sleep apnoea at a sleep study in four community cohorts and compares the odds of sleep apnoea across weight groups, so it is cross-sectional and gives no second line under rule T4 (one MR line; the Strong definition excludes cross-sectional data). GLP-1 trials lower the apnoea-hypopnoea index in people who already have sleep apnoea (another outcome, noted). No synthesis of prospective studies of BMI and new sleep apnoea was found. Lowered from Strong on 23 Oct 2026 (second check); the owner may restore Strong if a prospective synthesis is cited.

High LDL cholesterol → Peripheral artery disease

high_ldl|pad
FieldBeforeAfter
Trial and genetic evidenceTrial supportive; Genetic (MR) none; dose-response yesTrial supportive; Genetic (MR) supportive; dose-response yes

The cited CTT meta-analysis does not report peripheral arterial disease incidence per mmol/L, so the filed number had no support. The only published per-1-mmol/L estimate I found is the Mendelian randomisation one (2.09, 1.30-2.38), which reflects lifetime exposure and so exceeds any observational or trial-based figure; the observational contrast in the same paper is a hazard ratio of 1.41 (1.23-1.62) for LDL-C above the 95th percentile versus below the 50th. Whichever is published, the contrast label must say which. Added 20 Oct 2026 (review item 75): the estimate is itself a Mendelian randomisation result, so the genetic-evidence tag now reads supports. The abstract (PMID 31514949) prints the interval as 1.30 to 2.38. It is lopsided around 2.09 on the log scale, which may point to a misprint in the paper; it is shown as published. review_note

Current cigarette smoking → Asthma (adult)

smoking|asthma
FieldBeforeAfter
Trial and genetic evidenceTrial none; Genetic (MR) none; dose-response yesTrial none; Genetic (MR) supportive; dose-response yes

The stated 1.35 (1.22-1.49) for current versus never smokers, graded 'Probable', is contradicted by the largest pooled observational analysis available (231,020 participants across 22 population studies), which found exactly no association (OR 1.00, 0.91-1.09). Mendelian randomisation in the same consortium does suggest a small causal effect, but only 1.06 (1.01-1.11) per smoking-increasing allele. Smoking's well-documented effects on asthma control, severity and asthma-COPD overlap are being conflated here with an effect on asthma incidence. Added 20 Oct 2026 (review item 75): the displayed estimate is the observational one. The same paper's Mendelian randomisation analysis in current smokers found a higher asthma risk per smoking-increasing allele (OR 1.06, 95% CI 1.01-1.11; P = 0.020), so the genetic-evidence tag now reads supports. review_note

FieldBeforeAfter
Trial and genetic evidenceTrial contradicts; Genetic (MR) none; dose-response yesTrial contradicts; Genetic (MR) supportive; dose-response yes

Per-unit mismatch: no source reports a per-1-mg/dL estimate; the published figure is per 1 SD of genetically predicted urate, 1.19 (1.10-1.30). Low physical activity → Type 2 diabetes

low_pa|t2d
FieldBeforeAfter
Comparisonlowest vs highest total physical activity (inverse of the published high-vs-low estimate)lowest vs highest total physical activity

The proposed value is the exact inverse of Aune 2015's high-versus-low total physical activity estimate (1/0.65 = 1.54; 1/0.71 = 1.41; 1/0.59 = 1.69); the leisure-time-only estimate inverts to 1.35 (1.27-1.43), so the filed 1.45 sits between the two and matches neither. The cited DPP is a randomised lifestyle trial combining diet, exercise and weight loss and cannot support an observational inactive-versus-active contrast. The number shown is the inverse of the published high-vs-low estimate. review_note

Low whole grain intake → Type 2 diabetes

low_wholegrain|t2d
FieldBeforeAfter
Comparisonper 30 g/day lower whole grain intake (inverse of the published per-30 g/day estimate)per 30 g/day lower whole grain intake (hazard ratio)

The filed quantile figure is not traceable to any meta-analysis I found. The published high-quality evidence is dose-response, not categorical: 0.87 (0.82-0.93) per 30 g/day, which inverts to the proposed 1.15 (1.08-1.22). For scale, Aune 2013's dose-response gives 0.68 (0.58-0.81) per 3 servings/day, whose inverse is 1.47, so a lowest-versus-highest contrast could plausibly be anywhere between about 1.15 and 1.47 depending on the intake range assumed, which is why the per-unit form should be published instead. The number shown is the inverse of the published per-30 g/day estimate. review_note

Vitamin D deficiency → Type 2 diabetes

vitd_deficiency|t2d
FieldBeforeAfter
Comparisonlowest vs highest quartile of 25(OH)D (inverse of the published highest-vs-lowest estimate)lowest vs highest quarter of blood vitamin D

The filed 1.25 is the exact inverse of the per-1-SD observational estimate in Zheng 2020 ('each 1-standard deviation (SD) higher level of 25(OH)D was associated with a 20% lower risk of T2D (relative risk [RR]: 0.80; 95% CI 0.77, 0.84)'), carried on a lowest-versus-highest quantile label, a per-unit figure wearing a quantile contrast. The quartile contrast is much stronger at 1.69. Both are observational only: the same paper's Mendelian randomisation finds no causal effect (OR 0.96, 95% CI 0.89-1.03 per SD), matching the null supplementation trials, so Contested is the right grade whichever number is published. The number shown is the inverse of the published highest-vs-lowest estimate. review_note

Moderate alcohol use → Coronary heart disease

alcohol_moderate|chd

Link removed (rr 0.85 grade Contested).

9 Sep 2026 evidence audit: The August review marked this link for removal: Both cited sources contradict the direction on file. In the ADH1B analysis of 261,991 people the allele that LOWERS alcohol intake by 17% also LOWERS coronary heart disease risk (0.90, 0.84 to 0.96), and the authors conclude that reducing consumption is beneficial even for light-to-moderate drinkers; in China Kadoorie Biobank the conventional U-shape disappears entirely when genotype-predicted intake is used. A protective moderate-drinking link should not be published on a public site: the 'Contested' grade implies a live dispute, but the genetic evidence points one way and the observational protection is attributable to abstainer misclassification and confounding. If the link is kept at all it should be re-stated as no causal protective effect. corrections.json remove_links

Moderate alcohol use → Ischaemic stroke

alcohol_moderate|stroke_isch

Link removed (rr 0.95 grade Contested).

9 Sep 2026 evidence audit: The August review marked this link for removal: The cited China Kadoorie Biobank analysis states directly that the apparently protective effects of moderate alcohol against stroke are largely non-causal, and finds a continuously positive log-linear genetic association with ischaemic stroke, 1.27 (1.13-1.43) per 280 g per week. Publishing a protective moderate-drinking link for ischaemic stroke inverts the causal evidence. The Contested grade is too generous: the genetic evidence is one-directional. corrections.json remove_links

metabolic_syndrome|masld

Link removed (rr 3.8 grade Probable).

9 Sep 2026 evidence audit: The August review marked this link for removal: This link is close to circular and duplicates factors already listed. Under the 2023 MASLD nomenclature the diagnosis requires hepatic steatosis plus at least one cardiometabolic criterion, and those criteria are the components of metabolic syndrome (waist circumference, glucose, triglycerides, HDL, blood pressure), all of which appear elsewhere in this cluster as separate links. I could also find no cohort meta-analysis supporting 3.8 for incident disease. Recommend removing rather than adjusting, so the site does not double-count adiposity and diabetes. corrections.json remove_links

Low calcium intake → Osteoporotic fracture

low_calcium|fracture

Link removed (rr 1.15 grade Suggestive).

9 Sep 2026 evidence audit: The cited source reports no association on the stated contrast, or no comparative estimate. August review note: The definitive systematic review of this question found no association between dietary calcium intake and fracture in the great majority of cohort studies, and no pooled observational estimate is offered - so there is nothing to support 1.15 (1.05-1.26) for lowest versus highest intake. Randomised evidence points the same way: in the trials at lowest risk of bias (4 trials, n=44,505) calcium supplements had no effect on fracture at any site, and the apparent benefit in the wider trial set (0.89, 0.81-0.96) showed funnel-plot asymmetry consistent with publication bias. This link should probably be removed or regraded to Limited. corrections.json remove_links

Occupational noise → Age-related hearing loss

occ_noise|hearing_loss

Link removed (rr 2.2 grade Probable).

9 Sep 2026 evidence audit: The cited source reports no association on the stated contrast, or no comparative estimate. August review note: Two problems. First, the only pooled exposed-versus-unexposed figure I located is OR 4.46 for high-frequency noise-induced hearing loss, twice the filed value; the 2.20 that does appear in that literature is the contrast between non-Gaussian and Gaussian noise, not between exposed and unexposed, and the China meta-analysis's 2.26 is its male-versus-female odds ratio. Second, the outcome mapping is wrong in kind: occupational noise causes noise-induced hearing loss, a distinct entity from age-related hearing loss (presbycusis), and none of these meta-analyses report age-related hearing loss as the outcome. Note also that this link's triple (2.20; 1.85, 2.62) is byte-identical to hiv|ckd, which is not possible for two independently transcribed estimates. corrections.json remove_links

Link removed (rr 1.1 grade Probable).

9 Sep 2026 evidence audit: The cited source reports no association on the stated contrast, or no comparative estimate. August review note: The WHO-linked appraisal of concentration-response functions searched systematically and found no reviews at all for long-term ozone, concluding 'No specific suggestions were given for ozone because of the lack of relevant systematic reviews'. The 2024 WHO AQG update likewise associates long-term ozone only with respiratory MORTALITY, not with COPD incidence. WHO AQG 2021, the single source cited on this link, sets a peak-season ozone guideline from respiratory-mortality evidence and does not report a per-10-ppb COPD relative risk. A per-unit figure of 1.10 with an interval excluding the null has no located provenance; if the intent was the GBD ozone-COPD exposure-response curve, that should be cited explicitly and its wide uncertainty interval carried over. corrections.json remove_links

9 Sep 2026 evidence audit: The cited source reports no association on the stated contrast, or no comparative estimate. August review note: Contradicted by the only systematic review that pools this exact contrast. Filippini 2022 found no association for highest-versus-lowest greenness by either NDVI or land-use methodology, and reported a U-shaped dose-response with imprecise estimates. Individual cohorts are weaker than the filed figure too: UK Biobank gives HR 0.968 (0.938-1.000) per IQR of greenspace and 0.891 (0.804-0.989) for the top versus bottom quartile. Link removed (rr 1.12 grade Suggestive).

9 Sep 2026 evidence audit: The cited source reports no association on the stated contrast, or no comparative estimate. August review note: Contradicted by the evidence base rather than merely uncited. Both meta-analyses that pooled legumes against incident T2D found no significant association: Afshin 2014 (2 studies, 2746 events) and Schwingshackl 2017, which excluded legumes from its six significant food groups and graded the legume evidence 'low'. GBD 2021, the source cited on this link, pairs 'diet low in legumes' with ischaemic heart disease, not with diabetes. A significant CI that excludes the null (1.04-1.21) is therefore not transcribed from anywhere I could find. corrections.json remove_links

HIV infection → Chronic kidney disease

Link removed (rr 2.2 grade Probable).

9 Sep 2026 evidence audit: The cited source reports no association on the stated contrast, or no comparative estimate. August review note: The available meta-analysis (Ekrikpo 2018) estimates CKD PREVALENCE within HIV-positive populations and has no HIV-negative comparison group, so it cannot yield a relative risk. The HIV umbrella review of 55 physical-health outcomes graded none of them convincing and did not surface CKD among its stronger signals. Decisive for the audit: this link carries exactly the same rr and interval as occ_noise|hearing_loss (2.20; 1.85, 2.62), an unrelated exposure and outcome. Two independently transcribed estimates cannot coincide to three digits across all three numbers, so at least one of these was generated rather than read. corrections.json remove_links

Blood pressure treatment → Chronic kidney disease

antihypertensives|ckd

Link removed (rr 0.85 grade Convincing).

9 Sep 2026 evidence audit: The cited source reports no association on the stated contrast, or no comparative estimate. August review note: The most serious problem found in this cluster: the direction is contradicted by the trial the link cites. In participants without CKD at baseline, intensive systolic BP lowering INCREASED incident CKD (defined as a >30% eGFR fall to below 60) in both SPRINT and ACCORD - 3.5% versus 1.0% at three years in SPRINT, 10.0% versus 4.1% in ACCORD. Publishing 0.85 per 5 mmHg reduction as 'Convincing' protection against CKD, citing SPRINT, inverts the cited result. The eGFR fall is thought to be partly haemodynamic and may be reversible, and BP lowering does reduce cardiovascular events and ESRD progression in people who already have CKD - but that is a different population and a different outcome. This link should be withdrawn or restated as an effect on CKD progression in established CKD. corrections.json remove_links

Childhood obesity → Knee osteoarthritis

childhood_obesity|oa_knee

Link removed (rr 1.6 grade Suggestive).

9 Sep 2026 evidence audit: The August review marked this link for removal: No meta-analysis of childhood or adolescent obesity and incident knee osteoarthritis exists. The best available life-course evidence, the 1946 British birth cohort with ten BMI measurements from age 2 to 53, explicitly finds no additional risk from adolescent BMI once adult BMI is accounted for - that is, the exposure is a proxy for adult obesity, which is already published as a separate link in this dataset (high_bmi|oa_knee). Publishing both double-counts the same causal pathway. If the link is kept rather than removed it should carry no effect estimate and be marked as mediated by adult BMI. corrections.json remove_links

Heavy physical work → Osteoporotic fracture

heavy_work|fracture

Link removed (rr 1.2 grade Limited).

9 Sep 2026 evidence audit: The cited source reports no association on the stated contrast, or no comparative estimate. August review note: Contradicted by the largest study that has asked this question. The Women's Health Initiative Observational Study followed 93,676 postmenopausal women for a mean 11.5 years with 1,834 hip fractures, scored occupational physical demand from lifetime job histories, and found no overall association. I found no meta-analysis of heavy manual work and osteoporotic fracture at all, so 'n_reviews: 3' is unsupported. The direction is also contested a priori: mechanical loading raises bone density, which is why the general physical-activity literature finds fracture protection, and any excess would come from falls and trauma rather than from osteoporosis. corrections.json remove_links
